transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Democratic lawmakers are condemning President Trump's choice
of Stephen Miller as his next White House Chief of Staff.
Miller will replace Suzy Wilde Monday following Republicans' midterm losses.
Democratic Congressman Don Beyer criticized the appointment
during an interview with the BBC.
Stephen Miller is probably the single darkest force,
the Darth Vader of this country right now, of this presidential leadership.
What he's done with the cruel and chaotic immigration enforcement,
I hate to have that kind of ethic, those kinds of morals,
as the Chief of Staff for the president, but it's probably what Trump wants.
President Trump has repeatedly praised Miller's work,
calling him an MVP and one of his most trusted advisers.
Federal law enforcement have given little indication
they're investigating the deaths of nine people killed by ICE agents
since President Trump took office for the second time.
NPR's Meg Anderson reports the killings likely will be the targets
of renewed investigations when the new Congress convenes.
Once they have a majority in Congress,
Democrats say they plan to issue subpoenas to major players
in Trump's mass deportation plan,
compelling them to answer key questions under oath.
That could include Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen
and his predecessor Kristi Noem, among others.
Brent Ganger is the brother of Renee Good,
a U.S. citizen killed by an ICE officer in Minneapolis last January.
He says hearing more about his sister's death will be hard.
But I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day.
In a statement, DHS told NPR that Democrats are, quote,
"more interested in political shenanigans than in governing,"
but said the agency is prepared.
Meg Anderson, NPR News.
Two U.S. Senate races remain undecided as ballot counting continues.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colombe holds a narrow lead
over Republican Senator Cindy Hyde Smith.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is slightly ahead of Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin reports.
Alaska is about three times the size of France.
With few roads, mail is slow.
By law, the state allows up to 15 days for ballots to arrive.
If Peltola or Sullivan wins more than 50 percent of the vote, that's it.
They've won.
With four people on the ballot, though, it could come down to ranked choices.
That's like an instant runoff.
It takes just seconds for a computer to eliminate the losing candidate
and count the next choices on those ballots.
But the state only does it once the 15 days are up.
The Associated Press could call the race well before November 18.
Or, if it's close, not.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
This is NPR News.
New Zealand's two main political parties are neck and neck
as vote counting continues in the country's general election.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is seeking a second term in office
with former leader Chris Hipkins, his main opposition.
Adam Hancock is following the vote from Sydney, Australia.
This was predicted to be an extremely close race,
and the results so far indicate that the pre-election polls were correct.
The ruling centre-right national party are hoping to retain power,
but they are deadlocked with the centre-left Labour Party.
Coalition governments are the norm in New Zealand politics,
but this year's tight race means that one or more of the country's smaller parties
will likely play kingmaker to decide who governs.
Official results won't be announced until November 27,
with special votes, including those from overseas voters, still to be counted.
The election campaign has been dominated by cost of living concerns
with high unemployment and persistent inflation.
For NPR News, I'm Adam Hancock in Sydney.
We have joined evening prayers at the main cathedral in Montevideo on Friday.
He's in Uruguay at the start of a 12-day trip through South America.
Today's schedule includes Mass and a prayer vigil at a soccer stadium.
The Pope will also travel to Argentina and Peru,
where he served as a missionary and bishop.
The pontiff's trip comes weeks after the 71-year-old underwent surgery
with cancerous tumor on his lung.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Trump names Stephen Miller as next White House Chief of Staff, replacing Suzy Wiles
Democrats criticize Miller appointment; Rep. Don Beyer calls him the darkest force in the administration
Federal investigations into nine deaths by ICE agents unlikely; Democrats plan subpoenas to Mullin and Noem
Renee Good's brother says hearing about his sister's ICE killing will be hard
Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colombe leads Republican Cindy Hyde Smith as ballots are counted
Alaska Senate race: Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican Dan Sullivan; ranked-choice count pending
New Zealand election: Luxon's National Party and Labour under Hipkins deadlocked as votes are counted
Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay to begin 12-day South America trip, including Argentina and Peru
